title: 14-storey Carden Street tower proposal public meeting
subtitle: Habitat for Humanity Speedvale apartments approved, zoning housekeeping amendments passed, and a public spaces by-law adopted on a split vote.
overview: Council held a statutory public meeting on a proposal for a 14-storey building with 120 rental units and ground-floor commercial space at 26-40 Carden Street and 27-39 Macdonell Street. The downtown plan currently allows three to six storeys on the site. Council received the report {{vote:m4}} but made no decision. Staff will review the comments and bring back a recommendation, which they expect within a couple of months. A separate downtown height study is also under way, with a public meeting planned for December.

Council approved the Official Plan and zoning changes for a six-storey, 48-unit Habitat for Humanity apartment building at 303-317 Speedvale Avenue East, with 24 affordable units {{vote:m3}}. It also approved housekeeping zoning amendments for several sites that carry forward tribunal decisions and set placeholders for pending appeals {{vote:m5}}.

Council authorized notice of intention to designate 106 Carden Street under the Ontario Heritage Act {{vote:m2}}. It approved a by-law regulating the use of certain public property, with St. George's Square and Marco Square added as sensitive public spaces, on a split vote {{vote:m7}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Official Plan and zoning amendments for a six-storey, 48-unit Habitat for Humanity apartment building with 24 affordable units, and decided no further public notice is required.

decisions.item: 26-40 Carden St and 27-39 Macdonell St public meeting
decisions.detail: Council received the public meeting report on the proposed 14-storey, 120-unit mixed-use building; no decision was made and staff will bring back a recommendation.
Council approved city-initiated amendments that bring tribunal-approved zoning into the 2023 zoning by-law and add placeholders for properties still under appeal.
Council authorized the City Clerk to publish and serve notice of intention to designate the property, with the designation by-law returning if no objections are received in 30 days.
Council approved the by-law regulating use of certain public property as amended, with the vote split {{vote:m7}}.

debate: Several delegates and some councillors said a jump from six to 14 storeys departs from the downtown secondary plan, which came from long community consultation. They worried it would set a precedent for ad hoc site-specific approvals and change the human scale and heritage character of the core.

Supporters, including a nearby property owner and active transportation advocates, backed added density and rental housing near transit and welcomed the lack of car parking. Others, including a delegate who uses a walker, raised concerns about accessible parking, pick-up and drop-off, deliveries and traffic on Macdonell Street.

Delegates from the neighbouring non-profit building to the east asked for a design that would not block their future expansion. They raised concerns about reduced side yards, windows facing a blank wall, balconies near their rooftop, snow load, shading, construction impacts and the single loading bay. Staff said setbacks and effects on adjacent sites would be reviewed.

Delegates and councillors pressed for affordable units. The applicant said it could not commit to affordable units before site plan and funding are known. Staff noted the provincial affordability definition and said they would report back on development charge and parkland questions.

Many councillors said they supported housing and wanted to find a way to approve something. They urged staff and the applicant to work with neighbours and to consider the downtown height study. One suggested the applicant could defer, and staff said a written request would be needed.
